english_translation: I heard through rumors that the prices of goods in the shops keep rising nowadays.

dialogue.shona: Ndanzwa nerunyerekupe kuti mitengo yezvinhu muzvitoro iri kuramba ichikwira mazuva ano.
dialogue.english: I heard through rumors that the prices of goods in the shops keep rising nowadays.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Ndanzwa [ndanzwa] • nerunyerekupe [and / with runyerekupe] • kuti [that / so that] • mitengo [mitengo] • yezvinhu [yezvinhu] • muzvitoro [in / singular zvitoro] • iri [iri] • kuramba [to / at ramba] • ichikwira [ichikwira] • mazuva [plural zuva] • ano [ano]

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Connecting Clauses & Expressing Purpose with 'kuti'
grammar_notes.content: The connector 'kuti' is one of the most useful words in Shona. After verbs of speaking, thinking, or knowing (like 'akati' = said, 'unofunga' = you think, 'ndinoziva' = I know), 'kuti' means 'that'. However, when placed after an action verb, 'kuti' means 'so that / in order to', and the following verb changes its final vowel from '-a' to '-e'! For instance, '-dya' (eat) becomes 'kuti tidye' ('so that we may eat'), and '-wana' (get) becomes 'kuti uwane' ('so that you may get').
grammar_notes.rule: kuti + [Subject Prefix + Verb ending in -e] = 'so that [someone] may...' (e.g., kuti tidye = so that we eat)

grammar_notes.title: Joining Words with 'ne-' ('and / with') in 'nerunyerekupe'
grammar_notes.content: Look closely at 'nerunyerekupe'. In Shona, the word for 'and' or 'with' between nouns is not a separate word—instead, the prefix 'ne-' (or 'na-' before people's names) is written attached directly to the second noun! For example, 'ne-' + 'runyerekupe' forms 'nerunyerekupe'. You will see this everywhere in daily speech: 'sadza nemuriwo' ('sadza and vegetables'), 'nesimba' ('with strength'), and 'nekukasira' ('with haste / quickly').
grammar_notes.rule: ne- + Noun = and / with [Noun] (written as a single word, e.g., sadza nemuriwo = sadza and vegetables)

cultural_notes.title: Shop Prices ('Mitengo yeZvinhu') & Word-of-Mouth News ('Runyerekupe')
cultural_notes.content: Notice the expressive noun 'runyerekupe' ('word-of-mouth rumour / grapevine news'). Comparing shop prices ('mitengo yezvinhu muzvitoro') and sharing tips on affordable wholesalers is a staple of everyday conversation.

active_exercises.prompt: In 'Uya kuno undibatsire', what does the prefix '-ndi-' inside 'undibatsire' mean?
active_exercises.explanation: The object prefix '-ndi-' always means 'me', placed directly before the verb stem '-batsira' (help).

active_exercises.prompt: Translate this new polite request into English: 'Chimbomirira zvishoma pamusuwo.'
options: Come inside the house and sit on the chair.
Please wait a little while at the door.
Return home early before the sun sets.
Take your books and put them in the bag.
active_exercises.correct_answer: Please wait a little while at the door.
active_exercises.explanation: 'Chimbomirira' = 'Wait a little / for a moment right now', 'zvishoma' = 'a little', 'pamusuwo' = 'at the door'.

active_exercises.prompt: How do you say 'There is a cup of water on the table' in Shona?
active_exercises.explanation: 'Patafura' ('on the table') pairs with 'pane' ('there is at/on that spot') + 'kapu yemvura' ('a cup of water').
